title: Pliny the Elder's Historia Naturalis Catalogs Magic Practices
description: Pliny the Elder's encyclopedic Historia Naturalis (published c. 77 CE, though drawing on lifetime research) devotes substantial attention to magic practices, treating them as natural phenomena worthy of rational investigation and systematic debunking. Pliny simultaneously records magic practices as empirical data and condemns magic (magia) as the most fraudulent of arts. His work became one of the most-read classical texts throughout the medieval period, transmitting Roman knowledge of herb-lore, animal magic, and sympathetic magic to later European readers. Book 30 in particular provides an invaluable catalog of what Romans understood magic to consist of.
historiographical_note: Valerie Flint and Richard Gordon have both analyzed Pliny's treatment of magic as exemplary of Roman ambivalence — simultaneously empiricist documentation and moral condemnation — that shaped subsequent European engagement with magical practice.
source_method: Published scholarship; Pliny Natural History Books 28-30; secondary classical scholarship
